promo-info-red.title: Canva refuses the number and says nothing #shorts
promo-info-red.description:
Custom size. Nine hundred wide, six thousand tall — and the height field goes red the moment the number passes 3,125.

There is no warning text explaining why, no suggestion, no "would you like to scale this". It simply will not accept the number. Canva's maximum design size is 8000 × 3125 pixels, per axis, so that second number is your height ceiling — on the one format whose whole point is that it scrolls.

Now the fix, live. Halve it. 450 by 3000. Accepted immediately, because 3,000 is under the ceiling. Build the whole infographic at that size, then export at 2× and out comes the file you were told you could not make.

promo-info-maths.title: Design small, export big #shorts
promo-info-maths.description:
Canva lets you download a PNG at between 0.5 and 3.125 times the design size. That multiplier is the escape hatch, and almost nobody uses it deliberately.

So work backwards. Decide the pixels you actually want — say 900 wide by 6000 tall, a proper long one. 6,000 is over the ceiling, so halve both numbers: 450 by 3000. 3,000 is under 3,125, so Canva accepts it.

Build the whole thing at 450 × 3000. Then at download, PNG, and set the size multiplier to 2×. Out comes 900 × 6000. Same artwork. The ceiling never applied to the file, only to the canvas.

promo-info-shapes.title: Three sizes. None of them match. #shorts
promo-info-shapes.description:
Canva's own infographic page recommends three sizes. For a blog, 663 by 2000. For Facebook, 1200 by 628. For LinkedIn, 1104 by 736.

Read those again. The first is a tall column, three times higher than it is wide. The other two are landscape. They are not variations of each other — there is no single artwork that is both.

So stop trying to make one. The tall one is your master, where the whole argument lives. The landscape ones are extracts: one section, one number, one claim, re-laid out to fill a wide frame. Canva's Resize tool changes the canvas but does not re-think the layout.

promo-info-stamp.title: Zoom out to a postage stamp #shorts
promo-info-stamp.description:
Before you export, the test almost nobody does, and it costs ten seconds.

Zoom out until the whole infographic fits on your screen at about the size of a postage stamp. That is roughly what it looks like in a feed, or as a preview thumbnail, or in search results.

What should survive at that size: the shape of it, the colour blocks, and the biggest numbers. If all you can see is grey texture, the type is too uniform — the sizes are too close together and nothing is leading the eye. Go back and make the numbers bigger. Not the headings, the numbers.

And check the top two inches separately — often the only part that gets seen at all.
